Trench
trĕnch
n. (a ditch, an entrenchment; rendering Hebrew tealah and maagalah)
From Old French trenchier, to cut. A trench is a cut in the ground — made for defence, for siege, or for water.

Biblical Definition

A trench is a cut ditch. Elijah's is the most famous: on Carmel he repaired the altar, laid the wood, and “made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed” (1Ki 18:32), then filled it with water three times so that the fire's work could not be mistaken. Saul sleeps in one while David steals his spear (1Sa 26:5–7). Christ foretold Jerusalem's siege in the same vocabulary: “thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round” (Luk 19:43).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a trench as a long narrow cut in the earth; a ditch; and in fortification, a deep ditch cut for defence or for approaching a besieged place.

expand to see more

TRENCH, n. A long narrow cut in the earth; a ditch; as a trench for draining land.

2. In fortification, a deep ditch cut for defense, or to interrupt the approach of an enemy.

TRENCH, v.t. To cut or dig, as a ditch.

Key Scripture

1Ki 18:32 — "And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD: and he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed."

1Ki 18:38 — "Then the fire of the LORD fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench."

1Sa 26:5 — "And David arose, and came to the place where Saul had pitched: and David beheld the place where Saul lay, and Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host: and Saul lay in the trench, and the people pitched round about him."

Luk 19:43 — "For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,"

Modern Corruption

Christians look for ambiguous signs they can interpret generously, where Elijah engineered a test that would leave no room to explain the result away.

expand to see more

The trench on Carmel is a deliberate exclusion of every alternative explanation. Elijah could have simply prayed over dry wood; instead he dug a ditch, filled the trench with water, and drenched the sacrifice three times until the water ran round about the altar. When the fire fell it consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench. The extra water existed so that no one present could file the event under coincidence.

There is a discipline in that for anyone praying about a decision. Vague requests produce vague answers that confirm whatever the asker already wanted; Elijah's method was to make the conditions so adverse that a positive result could only be attributed to God. Luke 19:43 shows the word's other edge — Christ weeping over a city whose enemies would cast a trench about her, because she knew not the time of her visitation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tealah (H8585), a conduit or trench; maagalah (H4570), an entrenchment or wagon-track; Greek charax (G5482), a palisade or siege-mound.

expand to see more

Hebrew tealah (H8585) — conduit, trench; 1 Kings 18:32, 35, 38.

Hebrew maagalah (H4570) — entrenchment, track; 1 Samuel 26:5, Saul lay in the trench.

Greek charax (G5482) — palisade, siege-work; Luke 19:43, thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee.

Usage

"“He made a trench about the altar” — a test built to exclude coincidence."

"“Licked up the water that was in the trench” — the fire took even the obstacle."

"“Thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee” — Christ weeping over the siege to come."
